# Staying Compatible with the Reference Implementation

`foks-rs` is not the only FOKS. The reference implementation is written in
Go, lives at `github.com/foks-proj/go-foks`, and runs the public host at
`foks.app`. The Rust implementation targets a specific release of it,
v0.1.9, and must produce and consume bytes that Go code accepts, because
signatures, hashes, and Merkle leaves all commit to exact bytes. A Rust
client must be able to sign up against a Go server; a Go client must be
able to verify a Rust server's hostchain; and a Rust client that reads a
Go client's on-disk state must find the same keys. This chapter is about
how the project earns confidence in those claims and keeps it as upstream
changes.

## Two techniques from the testing literature

*Differential testing*, named by William McKeeman in 1998, tests a program
by giving the same input to two or more implementations of the same
specification and comparing their outputs. It needs no oracle that knows
the right answer, only the observation that if two independent
implementations disagree, at least one is wrong. McKeeman used it on C
compilers; it applies equally to serializers, verifiers, and protocol
handlers. Its weakness is that both implementations can share a mistake.
Here the comparison is deliberately asymmetric: the reference
implementation, not the specification, is the ground truth, because
interoperating with deployed Go code is the goal, whether or not Go matches
the spec.

*Golden testing* (also called fixture, snapshot, or characterization
testing) records an output once, stores it, and fails the test if the
output ever changes. Golden files are cheap and fast but only as
trustworthy as their provenance: a golden file produced by the code under
test proves nothing. The fixtures in this chapter were produced by the Go
implementation, and the manifests record enough to prove that.

The compatibility story has five rings, from cheapest and most hermetic to
most expensive and most realistic.

```
  Ring 1   protocol and method IDs        extracted from Go source by AST, pinned by hash
  Ring 2   Go-certified byte fixtures     checked-in bytes, manifests, re-serialization
  Ring 3   the Go oracle                  Go code re-verifies Rust output
  Ring 4   live mixed runs                Rust client on Go server; Go client on Rust server
  Ring 5   hosted canary                  daily lifecycle against foks.app, signed lease
```

## Ring 1: identifiers extracted, pinned, and ring-fenced

Every FOKS protocol has a 32-bit ID and every method a small integer
position, and these are the dispatch keys on the wire
([Chapter 17](17-wire.qmd)). Copying them by hand from Go source is
error-prone and, worse, silently wrong when upstream changes one.

`tools/foks-protocol-sync` is a Go program that uses only the standard
library. It parses the go-foks source with `go/parser` and `go/ast` and
never imports or executes an upstream package. From the generated protocol
files it extracts:

- protocol IDs from `var XxxProtocolID = ...` declarations, evaluated by a
  small constant evaluator;
- method positions from the single `NewMethodV2(protocol, position,
  "Proto.method")` call inside each generated client function;
- whether each protocol wraps its argument and result in `DataWrap`, by
  inspecting the types of the local variables the generator names `warg`
  and `tmp` (this is how the bare-payload team and Kex protocols were
  discovered);
- status codes and service types from the library's constant tables;
- for every `.snowp` schema file, two SHA-256 digests: one of the raw
  bytes and one of a *token-normalized* form.

The token-normalized digest strips comments and whitespace and
length-prefixes each remaining token, so reformatting a schema changes the
raw digest but not the semantic one, while renaming a field changes both.
The output is a JSON artifact with sorted collections, so extraction is
deterministic, and the generation script runs the extractor **twice** and
compares the two outputs byte for byte before accepting either.

The artifact's SHA-256 is pinned as a constant in `foks-protocol-metadata`,
and the artifact records the upstream module path, version, and `go.sum`
hashes it came from. Ordinary Cargo builds never run Go; they compile
checked-in generated files, and `generate-protocol.sh --check` fails CI if
any generated file is stale.

Local extensions to the protocol are ring-fenced so they can never collide
with a future upstream identifier:

| Local extension | Reserved range |
|---|---|
| Protocol IDs | `0xf04b0000` to `0xf04bffff` |
| Method positions | 65,536 to 131,071, names beginning with `foks` |

A weekly job re-extracts from upstream's current mainline (resolving the
remote `HEAD` to an immutable commit and fetching at depth 1) and
classifies every difference against the pinned artifact:

| Class | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `wire_breaking` | an ID, position, header flag, or result type changed on something Rust supports, or an identifier was reused for a different name |
| `behavior_review_required` | a schema whose semantic digest changed feeds a supported protocol |
| `additive` | a new protocol, method, or status |
| `outside_local_slice` | a change to something Rust does not implement |
| `source_only` | the raw digest changed but the semantic digest did not |

The job opens or updates a tracking issue with the report. This turns the
question "did upstream change something that matters?" into a triaged
answer rather than a diff to read.

## Ring 2: Go-certified byte fixtures

`tools/foks-v019-oracle` is a Go program that links the official v0.1.9
modules and writes fixtures under `crates/foks-snowpack/tests/fixtures/`.
It has two file classes. `.snowp` files pass through Go's own canonical
checker, `core.AssertCanonicalMsgpack`, and the writer refuses to emit one
that fails; every checked-in `.snowp` fixture is therefore certified
canonical by Go, not by Rust. `.frame` files are ordinary RPC frames and
are deliberately not so classified.

Before writing a probe capture, the oracle verifies the hostchain, the
public-zone signature, the Merkle root signature, and the binding between
root and hostchain using Go's verifiers. Only then does it write a
`manifest.json` listing every file's size and SHA-256 together with
provenance: host ID, hostchain tail, Merkle epoch, root-node hash, and the
independently computed prefixed hash of the whole root. The manifest
deliberately carries no self-asserted "verified: true" fields. Its
existence is the assertion, because it is written only after Go's checks
pass.

On the Rust side the tests check every manifest entry's size and digest,
require that the files on disk are exactly the set in the manifest (no
strays), and round-trip every `.snowp` file: decode, re-encode, compare
bytes. The typed decoders in `foks-proto` then decode the same fixtures
into structs and re-encode to the same bytes, which is the property that
matters for signatures. The RPC crate does the same for request frames:
the Rust encoder must reproduce Go's `probe-request.frame`, and a Go test
pins the Go side of that pair using Go's own generated descriptors.

The mutation fixtures (signup, device provisioning, revocation, key
rotation, chat, invitations, single sign-on) are generated with
deterministic randomness from a counter-seeded SHA-256 generator, and the
Go suite generates the corpus twice, requiring byte-identical output.
Fixtures also cover the negative space: `.frame` responses for error
statuses so that status decoding is tested against real Go bytes.

## Ring 3: the Go oracle re-verifies Rust output

Fixtures test that Rust can consume what Go produces. The reverse
direction, that Go accepts what Rust produces, needs Go code to run on Rust
output. The oracle does this in several places:

- The Rust server generates host-key add and revoke publications, and the
  oracle replays the resulting hostchain through Go's `core.PlayChain`.
- A Go test confirms, from Go's descriptors, that `Probe.probe` uses
  `DataWrap` and `TeamLoader.loadTeamChain` does not; this is the ground
  truth behind the Rust headerless predicates.
- Go's mock PIV bus generates YubiKey fixtures so hardware-key encodings
  ([Chapter 7](07-hardware-keys.qmd)) are covered without hardware.

## Ring 4: live runs in both directions

Two opt-in test suites run whole implementations against each other.

**Rust client on Go server.** A Go test boots the unmodified v0.1.9
integration environment, PostgreSQL in Docker via testcontainers included,
and hands the client side to a Rust binary that performs signup, chain
loading, PUK retrieval, key-value writes, cache-check synchronization,
realtime chat, and device pairing. One accommodation was necessary: the Go
test helper deliberately uses a 1024-bit RSA certificate for its probe
endpoint in test mode, and the Rust TLS library correctly rejects that key
size. The test replaces only that ephemeral leaf using the same official
helper's production-strength path; handlers, CAs, and hostchain material
remain those of the unmodified environment.

**Go client on Rust server.** Another Go test drives the official client
library against a Rust server: it probes, plays the Rust hostchain with
`core.PlayChain`, verifies the bootstrap Merkle root and public zone with
Go's checkers, then registers, relays a device-pairing session, and sends
logs. Further scripts cover chat, teams, invitations across mixed hosts,
single sign-on, MCP, and account flows.

All of these are gated by environment variables so `cargo test` and
`go test ./...` stay hermetic.

## Ring 5: the hosted canary

A daily job runs a key-value and onboarding lifecycle against the real
`foks.app` host with a disposable account. Its outcome is published as a
signed *compatibility artifact*, a small JSON document binding a strictly
increasing generation, the target host, the run ID, generation and expiry
times (at most 7 days apart), the pinned protocol-metadata digest, digests
of the mutation and read results, an outcome, a set of capabilities, and a
drift reason. Validation encodes the policy structurally: a `Compatible`
artifact must have non-empty capabilities and no drift reason; a `Drift`
artifact must have *empty* capabilities and a reason. An artifact reporting
drift is therefore structurally unable to grant anything. Clients that
consult the artifact learn whether the Rust implementation is currently
known to work against that host without trusting a mutable web page.

## Following upstream past the pinned release

The baseline stays v0.1.9, but go-foks main (`35dc037`, the unreleased
v0.1.10) already changes behaviour that peers observe. Two mechanisms let the
Rust implementation follow it without disturbing the pinned contract.

**Statuses newer than the baseline.** The pinned artifact cannot supply a
status that upstream added later, and it is not regenerated for one. The
handwritten policy (`crates/foks-server/protocol/policy-v1.toml`) instead
lists such codes in `[[post_baseline_status]]` tables, each with its alias,
upstream name, explicit value and the upstream revision that defines it.
Merging refuses an entry whose name or value the pinned artifact already
defines, so an entry can neither shadow nor reuse a baseline status; the
renderer emits the constant into `status_codes.rs` after the pinned ones,
with its provenance as a comment, and into `protocol-v1.toml`. The drift
extractor treats these names as statuses the Rust code depends on. When the
baseline moves to a release that contains a status, its entry becomes an
ordinary alias. The two entries today are
`TEAM_VO_BEARER_TOKEN_NOT_FOUND_ERROR` (7016, `5a9ff13`) and
`RT_MSG_REPLAY_MISMATCH` (12007, `b41b354`).

**Fixtures generated from main.** `tools/foks-main-oracle` links the
pseudo-version of go-foks main and writes frames under
`crates/foks-snowpack/tests/fixtures/foks-main/<area>/`, each directory with
a README naming its generator and a `SHA256SUMS` file. The v0.1.9 fixture
tree is not touched.

Behaviour adopted from main so far:

- **KV creation results (`fd03098`, `b3c9177`).** go-foks main returns
  `KVMkdirRes` and `KVPutSmallFileOrSymlinkRes`, one-field structs whose
  `wasReplay` reports that an object with the same ID and identical
  persisted contents already existed, where v0.1.9 returns void. The Rust
  client decodes both shapes (an omitted result is `wasReplay = false`), and
  the Rust server returns the struct, which v0.1.9 clients accept because
  they decode a void result into an untyped value. A replay is not charged
  against usage; an ID reused with different contents is `KV_RACE_ERROR`
  with upstream's message. The policy lists the struct results under
  `accepted_upstream_results`, so the drift report classifies the result
  change as additive.
- **Grown realtime structs and send replays (`b41b354`, `c334c97`).**
  `RTSendRes` gains `wasReplay` and `RTChannelMetadata` gains `noPush`. Both
  decode as optional trailing fields that default to false, unknown later
  fields are retained, and the Rust implementation emits a flag only when it
  is set or was decoded, so bytes sent to v0.1.9 peers do not change. The
  server stores and re-serves channel metadata including any retained tail.
  A replayed send returns `wasReplay = true`; a send whose message ID is
  already held by a different message is `RT_MSG_REPLAY_MISMATCH` (12007,
  void payload), which the client treats as a definite rejection. The Rust
  rule for "the same message" is stricter than upstream's: the channel, the
  sender and the whole send envelope except `expectedPrevSeq` must match,
  whereas go-foks main (`loadReplay` in `server/realtime/messages.go`)
  compares only host, channel and sender and answers any other resend under
  the same ID as a replay. go-foks clients resend the stored envelope byte
  for byte, so no current client observes the difference.
- **Pegged messages (`bf9ace5`).** Replies, reactions and edits from go-foks
  main clients are authenticated and count toward history continuity, and
  the desktop shows them as placeholders naming the action; an edit with an
  empty body is shown as a deletion. The Rust server accepts pegged sends
  into Basic (format 1) channels and stores them as opaque sealed messages,
  as go-foks main does (`insertMessage` in `server/realtime/messages.go`).
  Neither server can open the body, so neither checks that its arm or
  target agrees with the metadata type; readers refuse a mismatch. Writer
  role, encryption role and current key, idempotent replay on the message
  ID, `expectedPrevSeq` and the size limits apply as for Basic, and the
  channel's last-message record takes its type from the metadata. The Rust
  server keeps its stricter Basic metadata checks for pegged sends (non-zero
  message ID, a predecessor sequence and ID that are both zero or both name
  the stored message, no `furtherUserAttribution`), which go-foks main
  clients satisfy. It accepts only Basic, Reply, Reactji and Edit: go-foks
  main stores any type from Basic to Leave, but the other types have no
  body arm, so no client can open them, and System, Join and Leave are
  meant for server-authored messages; the Rust server refuses them with
  `BAD_ARGS`. For type `None` go-foks main returns `PROTO_DATA_ERROR`
  (1035) and the Rust server `BAD_ARGS` (1030); a type past Leave fails
  argument decoding (`BAD_ARGS`). Both are definite rejections to a go-foks
  main client, and no client sends them. Accepting pegged kinds is not
  gated by a capability on either side; the Rust `content_actions` chat
  capability describes content actions in extended (format 2) channels,
  stays false, and is unaffected. The Rust client still does not compose
  pegged messages. v0.1.9 clients cannot open pegged messages, on a
  go-foks main host or a Rust host alike.
- **Unknown team view tokens (7016).** A go-foks main server answers a
  view-only team bearer token it holds no row for with
  `TEAM_VO_BEARER_TOKEN_NOT_FOUND_ERROR` (void payload), and its client then
  activates a new view and replays the operation once. The Rust server
  returns 7016 where it holds no row for the token (never issued, evicted or
  reclaimed after expiry) and `TEAM_BEARER_TOKEN_STALE_ERROR` where a row
  exists but has expired or its membership was superseded; earlier it
  returned `EXPIRED_ERROR` on the KV, chain-load and user-load paths. The
  stale status stays wherever a row exists because v0.1.9 Go clients
  recover only from that one (in their realtime sender lookup); to them 7016
  is an unknown status. On the client side, a team KV write session that
  receives either status activates one replacement view through the team
  loader and replays the refused request; the replacement is used only if
  the reloaded team opens exactly the same team keys. This covers the KV
  commands, adapter data writes and the root write after team creation. It
  cures a view the server reclaimed or let expire, and any refusal without a
  key change. A role change rotates or adds team keys, so after one the
  replacement is refused, nothing is replayed and the session returns the
  server's refusal; the caller must reload the team and start again, as the
  sealed material of the old session belongs to the old keys. Cached reads in the
  agent already retried on the stale and expired statuses and now also on
  7016. The bytes are checked against a main-generated frame.
- **Ownerless teams (`df2acf1`).** A new edit that takes the roster from at
  least one owner to none is refused locally by the Rust team editor (the
  counterpart of go-foks `GameplanOpts.RequireOwner`) and by the Rust server
  with `TEAM_ROSTER_ERROR` and upstream's message, "edit would leave team
  without an owner". The server check runs on the decoded change before
  link verification so that the status matches go-foks; `foks_verify` would
  otherwise refuse the link with a generic team error. Admitting a remote
  user's RSVP when that user is already in the roster is refused, as go-foks
  `TeamAdmit` refuses it; local users and teams were already refused. One
  difference remains: go-foks replays an existing chain that left its team
  without an owner, while `foks_verify` refuses such a link in replay as
  well, so a team that go-foks stranded does not load in a Rust client.

## Decoding structs that upstream grows

go-foks extends positional structs by appending fields, and its generated
code tolerates both directions: go-codec ignores array elements beyond the
fields a struct declares and decodes missing trailing fields as zero values.
Upstream documents the convention in the field comments of `wasReplay` and
`noPush` ("old servers omit the field"). A Rust decoder that insists on an
exact field count turns each such addition into an interoperability break,
as the realtime results in go-foks main showed. The Rust decoders therefore
follow one rule, stated in `crates/foks-proto/src/trailing.rs`:

- **Canonical objects decode exactly.** A struct that is signed, hashed,
  MAC'd, used as a key-derivation or nonce input, sealed as a box plaintext,
  or digested by a server keeps its exact field count, as does every struct
  nested inside one. Rust-only extensions that carry their own version number
  and are specified to fail closed (`RtChatCapabilities`) are also exact.
  Where a canonical object is already designed to grow (the Merkle root and
  public zone inside their signed blobs, the optional certificate name), its
  decoder accepts the documented lengths and the verifier checks signatures
  over the bytes it received.
- **Unsigned RPC arguments and results accept a trailing tail.** They require
  their known fields and accept any number after them.
- **The tail is retained wherever the receiver encodes the value again**:
  when it stores it, re-serves it, forwards it or compares it as bytes.
  Types that keep their decoded bytes (`KvListResponse`, `KvGetResponse`,
  `KvDirectoryPair`, `UserChain`, `TeamChain`) retain it in those bytes;
  `RtChannelMetadata` and `ChatSendReceipt` retain it in a `TrailingFields`
  value. A value that is only read may discard the tail; those decoders call
  `unsigned_rpc_fields`.

Encoders do not change: a value the Rust code constructs encodes exactly the
fields the pinned release defines, so v0.1.9 peers receive the same bytes as
before. `crates/foks-proto/tests/forward_tolerance.rs` checks, for v0.1.9
fixtures and constructed values, that each converted decoder still
re-encodes the original bytes, accepts appended fields and (where required)
retains them, and still refuses a missing field, and that canonical objects
refuse an appended field.

The audit applied this rule to every typed decoder in `foks-proto`:

| Area | Tolerant (unsigned RPC) | Exact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Realtime | channel set, inbox key, delta, channel and poll result, thread query and range, message list, thread page, last-message record, method argument wrappers other than the send argument; `RTSendRes` and `RTChannelMetadata` with retained optional fields | message metadata, noncer, message, message box, body, wrapper, ciphertext (hashed or nonce inputs); `RtSend` and its argument wrapper (the server compares the send for replay); name box and role pair inside re-served metadata; chat capabilities (versioned extension) |
| KV | get, list and directory-pair responses (retained), extended dirent, usage, encrypted chunk, path version vector | root, directory, dirent, small-file box, large-file metadata (MAC'd or stored and compared); upload chunk (digested by the server); small-file plaintext |
| Teams, invitations, federation | certificate lookup result, inbox pagination, inbox rows, remote view-token set, chain responses (retained), team edit result, team configuration, activated view | certificates, invites, permission payloads, view tokens, removal MACs and boxes, challenges, join-request payloads; the stored remote join request |
| Users, SSO, KEX, configuration | login result, username change, client version, version info, device nag, SSO configuration, token set, poll result, session and login arguments, KEX relay arguments, registration and host configuration, user lookup, Merkle lookup and historical-root results | chain links, HEPKs, reservations, invite codes, OAuth2 bindings, PPE boxes and parcels, key boxes, KEX wrapper and cleartext, YubiKey values, identity-status proofs |

Mutation arguments that carry signed links and canonical zero fields (signup,
provisioning, team creation and edits, revocation, passphrase updates), the
hand-written server argument decoders in `foks-rpc`, and the realtime send
argument are still exact; converting them requires deciding how the server
treats a tail it would store or compare.

The drift extractor records the positional layout of every generated go-foks
struct in a separate artifact, `upstream-v0.1.9-structs.json`, so that the
pinned protocol artifact and its digest (which hosted compatibility
artifacts commit to) are unaffected. `diff` reports fields appended to an
unchanged prefix as `struct_grown`: additive when the policy lists the struct
in a `[[tolerant_struct]]` table, review-required otherwise. A removed,
renamed, retyped or reordered field is `struct_changed`. Against go-foks main
(`35dc037`) the two grown structs, `RTSendRes` and `RTChannelMetadata`, are
classified as tolerated growth.

## Quirks preserved bug-for-bug

Differential testing finds the places where the reference implementation
does something the specification would not predict. The project preserves
them, because a Rust implementation that was "more correct" than Go would
be incompatible with it.

**Bare payloads for team and Kex protocols.** Described in
[Chapter 17](17-wire.qmd): five client-to-server protocols (31 methods) omit
the `DataWrap` envelope because their `.snowp` declarations omit the
`argHeader` and `resHeader` modifiers; the generator treats every file the
same way. Found by AST inspection, pinned by a Go test. Unchanged in go-foks
main as of `35dc037` (2026-10-11): `proto-src/rem/team.snowp`,
`proto-src/rem/kex.snowp`, `proto/rem/gen.go` and the `go-snowpack-compiler`
version are identical to v0.1.9.

**The Merkle epoch limit at 65,536.** Go's canonical checker for signed
objects rejects any `array16` with 31 or fewer elements, even though
MessagePack has no shorter encoding for 16 to 31 elements
([Chapter 9](09-canonical-encoding.qmd)). The skip-pointer list of a Merkle
root ([Chapter 12](12-epochs.qmd)) grows with the number of trailing zero
bits in the epoch, so it first reaches 16 entries at epoch 65,536 and has
16 or more at every later multiple of 32,768. A root at such an
epoch could not be encoded in a form Go would accept as signable, and since
roots are sequential no later epoch can be reached either. The cause is one
bound in `lib/core/snowp.go`: the `mpArray16` case rejects lengths up to
`0x1f`, the `str8` bound, where the fixarray bound is `0x0f`. Rust therefore
refuses to build back-pointer arrays of 16 to 31 entries and exposes
`MAX_CANONICAL_MERKLE_EPOCH = 65,536` as a documented limit rather than
silently diverging. Unchanged in go-foks main as of `35dc037` (2026-10-11):
v0.1.9..main touches no canonical encoding code in `lib/core` (`snowp.go`,
`crypto.go`, `sigs.go` and `sigs2.go` are identical) and nothing in
`lib/merkle`.

**Rotated invitation certificate signature order.** A team certificate for
an invitation carries stacked signatures ([Chapter 15](15-teams.qmd)). When
the team's admin key has rotated since the certificate was first issued,
the pinned v0.1.9 Go client verifies the signatures in the reverse of the
order in which they were applied (`[current PTK, generation-1 PTK]`), so it
cannot open any rotated certificate, whether a Go or a Rust host issued it.
Rust signs and verifies in the stacked order. The Rust fixture test decodes Go's
`rotated` certificate, re-creates it byte-exactly, and asserts that swapping
the two signatures makes verification fail. go-foks fixed its verifier in
`e07f30b` (#350, after v0.1.9): `openCert` now delegates to
`team.OpenTeamCert` and uses the stacked order, so Go clients built from main
open Rust-issued rotated certificates. Only the pinned v0.1.9 client still
has the quirk; the fixture test stays.

**Seed-chain receiver binding.** When a team's shared key rotates, Go builds
one seed chain per rotation and binds its informational "receiver" field
to the editor who performed the rotation, then attaches that same chain to
every recipient's parcel. Rust's decoder documents this and requires the
caller to bind each recovered seed to the authenticated team-chain key
history instead of trusting the field.

**The founding link's sequence number.** The Go `TeamCreator` emits a
founding membership link with its sequence number unset (zero) although
the team link itself is sequence one. The fixtures retain it so Rust can
decode Go history losslessly, but Rust is not permitted to emit it.

## Reading a Go client's state

Compatibility extends to the disk. `foks-go-interop` lets the Rust agent
discover, and on macOS import, credentials from an existing go-foks
installation. The Go secret store is a Snowpack document decoded with the
same canonical decoder, with a 16 MiB size cap, a cap of 256 candidate
credentials, `O_NOFOLLOW` on open, and a same-inode check to detect
concurrent modification. Go's "hard state" SQLite database is opened
read-only with `trusted_schema = OFF`, `query_only = ON`, and caps of 1,024
rows and 64 KiB per value, and each row's scoped key is recomputed with the
same typed hash Go used, so a row is accepted only if it really belongs to
the identity it claims. The macOS Keychain bundle is an XSalsa20-Poly1305
secretbox whose 24-byte nonce begins with the big-endian type ID, the
same domain-separated-nonce convention as the wire cryptography.
